Authorized the Defense Department to spend its own funds helping the former Soviet republics secure, transport, and dismantle nuclear, chemical, and other weapons after the Soviet collapse.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: 105 Stat. 1691](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/105/1691){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 22 U.S.C. 2551 note; 50 U.S.C. 3701 et seq.](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/22/2551?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Initial authority to transfer up to $400 million from defense accounts.
- Assistance for destroying weapons, safeguarding them in transit and storage, and preventing proliferation.
- Conditions on recipients, including commitments to arms control compliance.
- Later widened to cover biological threats and countries outside the former Soviet Union.

## Why it matters

It helped remove nuclear weapons from Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Belarus and is the standard example of defense spending used for prevention. Its annual funding and limits were set through [the annual NDAA](ndaa-annual.qmd).

## Current status

The program continues as the Defense Department's Cooperative Threat Reduction program, restated in permanent law in the FY2015 defense authorization. Cooperation with Russia itself ended in the 2010s.

[Last checked November 10, 2026.]{.checked}
